p: There are places in this world, and this is one of them, that seem to have been built by someone who loved them very much. The Bramble Grove was such a place — a small corner of forest where the sunlight came down between the leaves in patches, like it had been poured rather than shone, and where the wind, if you listened closely enough, seemed to be humming something it had learned a very long time ago and never quite forgotten. It was not a large place, the Bramble Grove. But to those who lived there, it was the entire world, and that is a very different thing from being large. The roots of the oldest trees ran deep and tangled beneath the paths, flowers grew up between the stones as if they'd been asked to, and every single morning — without fail, without exception, and without so much as a by-your-leave — the grove woke up loudly. Birds sang from branches that had heard the same songs a thousand times and never tired of them. Rabbits did whatever it is rabbits do when they think no one's watching, which is mostly just more of what they do when someone is. And the streams talked to themselves the whole way through the trees, the way streams do. Beneath the very tallest of those trees lived a young bear named Bearly. Now, Bearly was, by nature, an uncomplicated sort of bear. He did not yet know what it meant to be afraid, or lonely, or lost, because none of those things had introduced themselves to him yet. His home was warm. His belly was, more often than not, full. And every morning arrived carrying some new small adventure, waiting patiently just outside his door like a friend who's arrived a bit early. The best of these adventures, without question, was the one he shared every single day with a clever, quick, endlessly curious fox named Frederick. They were, the two of them, almost entirely unalike, which — as anyone who has ever had a best friend can tell you — is usually a very good sign. Frederick was fast and sharp-eyed, forever turning over leaves and peering under stones as though the forest owed him an explanation. Bearly was bigger, slower, and cheerfully clumsy, the sort of bear who fell into rivers not because he wasn't careful, but because he had gotten distracted by something interesting on the opposite bank. Frederick thought quickly. Bearly cared quickly. And between the two of them, not much in the Bramble Grove went unnoticed or unloved. They climbed trees they had no business climbing. They followed streams well past the point where following streams was sensible. They found secrets that, as far as they could tell, the forest had been keeping just for them. To Bearly, the Bramble Grove was not simply a place. It was the place — the one against which every other place would, for the rest of his life, quietly be measured. Which is, as it turns out, an important thing to know about a home. You rarely notice you've measured everything against it until the day it isn't there to measure against anymore. For generations, the creatures of the grove had lived beneath the shelter of the old trees, and had believed — as creatures with good homes tend to believe — that the grove would simply always be there. That home was not the sort of thing that could be lost. They were wrong. One morning, without any warning at all, the sky changed color. The birds, who had never once in living memory failed to sing, stopped. The wind went quiet, the way a room goes quiet when someone has said something nobody expected. And from the treeline came strange shapes — small, bright, bouncing things that might, from a great enough distance, have looked almost cheerful. They did not stay looking cheerful for long. Wherever these creatures landed, the world around them changed. Flowers wilted where they touched. Paths vanished beneath something thick and glistening. The streams, which had never stopped talking in all of Bearly's memory, went silent beneath a slick, unfriendly slime. The animals called it, simply and without much imagination, the Slimefall. They fought it, of course — every creature that could fight, fought. But the slime did not fight back so much as it simply continued, the way a tide continues, indifferent to how hard you push against it. Bit by bit, the home that had sheltered them for so long was taken from them, not violently, but patiently, which is somehow worse. Bearly was only a cub. Too small to fight. Too young, really, to understand what was happening at all. All he knew — the only thing he knew, in fact, with any certainty — was that the place he loved was disappearing, tree by tree, in front of him. And then, on the morning the last of the safe trees began to wither, Bearly and Frederick were made to leave. Two friends. One small bear. One clever fox. And, for the first time in either of their lives, no home to go back to. That was the day Bearly became, in the plainest and saddest sense of the words: A bear without a home.

c.t: The Gap Between Two Boys and Two Grown-Ups
p: Time, it should be said, is a very generous thing. It rarely announces itself. It simply passes, quietly, in the background of every conversation, until one day you look up and realize the cub you remember has become someone quite different — taller, steadier, and carrying, if you looked closely, the faint outline of everything he's lost. Years went by in the way years do — slowly when you're living through them, and all at once when you look back. Bearly grew. Frederick grew faster, in the particular way clever foxes tend to, and somewhere along the road from cub to grown bear, Frederick had become something else entirely: the leader of the small, hard-won village the two of them and a handful of other refugees from the Bramble Grove had built at the edge of the safe forest. It suited him, mostly. Frederick had always liked having a plan, and now he had an entire village's worth of plans to keep track of. Bearly, for his part, had grown into a bear who was still — underneath the size and the years — recognizably himself. Big. A little clumsy. Quick to care, slow to complain, and still, if you asked anyone in the village, entirely capable of losing an afternoon to a butterfly. "What more could you possibly want?" Frederick asked him one morning, the two of them sitting on the edge of the new garden wall, the way they had a hundred mornings before. "Life is good here, Bearly. We built this. You helped build this." "I know," Bearly said, and meant it. "I don't know. Something's still — missing. I can't tell you what." Frederick, who had learned a great many things about leading a village and precisely nothing about explaining a feeling like that, did the sensible thing and changed the subject. "Well," he said, "in the meantime, we need more berry bushes for the eastern garden, and you, my friend, happen to be the best berry-finder this village has ever produced. Would you go find us some?" Bearly agreed — of course he agreed, it was berries, how hard could it possibly be — and set off toward the forest's edge with every intention of coming straight back. Every intention, it must be said, is a wonderful thing to have. It is a much less reliable thing to keep, particularly for a bear whose attention has, since roughly the day he was born, had a weakness for anything that flies and glimmers. A butterfly happened, as butterflies do, and Bearly forgot the berries, the garden, and very nearly his own name, chasing it deep into a part of the forest that did not, strictly speaking, appear on any of the village's maps. It was there, an hour and one lost butterfly later, that something glinted at him from between the trees. "Ha," Bearly said to no one, grinning. "Maybe it's buried treasure." And, laughing at his own joke — because someone had to — he went to go find out.

Now, this next part you may have heard a piece of already — the sword, the ruin, the slime that appeared out of nowhere with all the manners of an uninvited guest. But every good story is worth hearing properly the second time, particularly when the first telling left out how the morning actually began. It had, as these things always seem to, started as a perfectly ordinary day. Bearly woke, stretched, ate his breakfast, and was halfway to the river to skip stones when a familiar voice stopped him cold. "Hey — listen!" Bearly turned, rolling his eyes with theatrical patience. "Oh. Hello, Great and Wise Leader of the Village. To what do I owe this tremendous honor?" Frederick scoffed and punched him lightly on the arm. "Where were you last night? We had the garden meeting." "Was that last night?" Bearly considered this seriously. "I thought I saw a butterfly. Followed it for a while, ended up out by the old tree. The stars were out. I think I saw a shooting star, actually." "Of course you were chasing butterflies," Frederick said, laughing. "You ever going to catch one?" "One of these days," Bearly said, with the total, unbothered confidence of a bear who has said this many, many times before and believed it every single time. Frederick told him, again, about the garden expansion and the berries, and Bearly — sighing with enormous, performative reluctance — agreed to go looking, because what else was he going to do, disappoint the Great and Wise Leader? He hadn't gotten far before the butterfly found him. Gold, unmistakably gold, drifting along like it had all the time in the world, which, as far as it knew, it did. Bearly followed it without a second's hesitation, the way he always did, the way he probably always would. He lost it near the brambles. He found, in its place, a glint. A wiser creature — and there is no shame in saying Bearly was not always the wisest creature in any given forest — might have wondered why a glint was glinting in a stretch of woods nobody had walked through in years. Bearly wondered only whether it might, at long last, be treasure. What it turned out to be was a ruin, quiet and ancient and clearly keeping a secret it had kept for a very long time, and at its heart, on a stone pedestal, a sword. Old. Rusted through in places. Not, by any reasonable measure, impressive. Bearly did not have a reasonable measure handy. "Ha!" he said, hoisting it triumphantly overhead. "Treasure! I am now a brave adventurer! No foe shall stand before me!" The forest, which up to that point had been listening politely, chose that exact moment to go very quiet. Bearly noticed a beat too late, the way you notice a held breath only after you've been holding it. He looked around properly for the first time. The trees here were darker than he remembered. The path behind him had gotten harder to find. "Where... am I?" he asked, which was an entirely reasonable question, and would — in time — turn out to have a considerably less reasonable answer. Then came the rustle. "Oh, come on," Bearly said to the bushes, as though they might listen to reason. "I didn't mean any of this." The bushes did not listen to reason. Out hopped a small green slime, dreadfully unimpressed by his protests, and Bearly did the only sensible thing available to a bear in his position — he ran, sword still clutched in one paw, dignity left somewhere back by the pedestal. He did not notice, as he ran, that the forest around him was changing. He noticed only that the slime was hopping after him at a pace no slime had any right to manage, and that looking back over his shoulder to check on it was — as it turns out — an excellent way to trip over a root. He threw his hands up. He closed his eyes. He felt something sticky. When he opened them again, the slime was no longer a slime so much as a stain, and Bearly realized, with some surprise, that he had never once let go of the sword. "Yuck," he said, with feeling, and wiped it off on the grass. "What on earth just happened?" Looking around, properly this time, he began to notice things. A familiar tree — the one he and Frederick had climbed, once, to spy on some squirrel babies, and both fallen out of, and both broken an arm on, and both, eventually, laughed about for a full year afterward. A familiar stump, worn smooth from years of small creatures sitting on it to hear stories. And, further on, a great mossy tree with a hollow at its base that Bearly recognized — slowly, the way you recognize an old friend's voice before you place their face — as somewhere he used to sleep, a very long time ago, before the Slimefall took it from him. "I could use a nap," he admitted to no one. "...Maybe I shouldn't." He napped anyway.

If you have never met a traveling merchant, you have missed out on one of the great pleasures of the world — the particular kind of person who has been everywhere, sold everything, and is nonetheless still faintly surprised by whatever he finds around the next bend. Micah the Merchant had always loved traveling more than selling. Selling was simply the excuse. It was the road itself he loved — the rediscovering of things that had once been lost. So it was that one morning, a tune he half-remembered drifted through his mind like something heard long ago and never quite forgotten, and he found himself thinking, could it truly be? — and setting off, on the strength of nothing more than a feeling, toward a forest he had not visited in years. Days later, he found a freshly cleared path leading into woods that still, in places, bore the scars of the Slimefall. "How long has it been," he murmured, hitching his pack higher, "since I was last here? And who, I wonder, has been clearing it?" The answer, when he found it, was sitting beside a tree, carefully cleaning an old, rusted sword. "Ah," Micah said. "So I was right." Bearly startled and turned. "Oh! My apologies — I didn't hear you arrive." "Nonsense," Micah said, waving a hand. "That is a rather peculiar sword you have there." Bearly glanced down at it fondly — a bear's head for a pommel, a paw print worked into the hilt guard. "This old thing? It was rusted through when I found it. I've been cleaning it up bit by bit. Funny — even old, forgotten things can turn out useful." "I'm sure you've been useful to it, as well, young one," Micah said, with the particular knowing smile of a man who has traveled far enough to recognize when something more than luck is at work. "I'm Micah. A traveling merchant. Might I set up shop here a while? Lovely clearing you've got." Bearly considered the clearing — his clearing, though he hadn't quite thought of it that way until just now — and pointed toward the old stump. "Should be safe enough. Set up there." Over the fire that evening, Micah asked what had brought a bear this deep into a forest that, by all accounts, ought to have been abandoned. "I'm not sure," Bearly admitted slowly. "At first, I was lost. Now... I'm honestly not sure anymore." They traded a coin for a fishing pole — an old coin Bearly had found lying near a felled slime, which Micah accepted with a smile that suggested he knew rather more about it than he was letting on — and Bearly spent the evening catching fish while turning the last few days over in his mind. Waking hungry. Wandering, half by memory, toward the blackberry patch he'd known as a cub. Meeting another slime, and this time keeping his eyes open, and slapping it away with the sword, more by luck than skill. More had come after that first one. He'd fought them all. Somewhere in the fighting, the sword had stopped feeling like a stranger's tool and started feeling, oddly, like it wanted to be swung. He didn't mention that part to Micah. Not yet.

Bearly woke the next morning to an empty clearing and a note pinned under a rock: Be back soon. Need new pots. He laughed, wondered which direction the merchant had gone, and — since no one had thought to leave him directions out of the forest either — picked a way he hadn't walked yet and set off to see where it led. It led, as it happened, somewhere darker. The rustling that met him this time did not belong to one small green slime, but to several — bigger than any he'd faced, nearly his own size. Bearly's breath caught, and something rose up in him that he did not recognize: not quite fear, not quite anger, something closer to instinct. He let out a roar he did not know he had in him. The slime hesitated. Bearly attacked. It fell apart beneath the sword — and split, astonishingly, into three smaller slimes, which he dispatched with the same startled thoroughness. "What in the — " he managed, before more rustling interrupted the thought entirely, and the sword, for just a moment, seemed to shimmer. Did the sword just — do something? he wondered, but there wasn't time to wonder for long, and he spent the rest of the day clearing slimes and asking the question again and again without ever quite answering it. When he returned to the clearing that evening, Micah had returned too — with company. A frog, cheerful and green, introduced himself with a flourish. "Henry's the name, and selling fish is the game," he said, and laughed heartily at his own rhyme before Bearly had finished deciding whether it was actually funny. "Isn't it dangerous out here?" Bearly asked. Micah and Henry exchanged a look, and then both laughed. "You say that," Henry said, "standing there with a mighty fine weapon." Bearly, muttering something about still being lost, went to go catch fish instead, which seemed a much simpler problem.

Two days can be a very long time, or a very short one, depending entirely on what fills them. These two were filled with small talk, small trades, and a curious game involving a ball, a pyramid of pegs, and considerably more betting than either bear or merchant would probably admit to. ("Plinko," Micah called it, with the fond authority of a man who had definitely lost money to it before and would definitely lose money to it again.) Five days after meeting Henry, Bearly woke to voices outside his den — Henry back again, sharing something hot with Micah, and two new faces besides: a solidly built beaver named David Bobby, and a sharp-eyed cat named Jasmine. "You sleep in that thing?" David asked, eyeing the tree hollow with open skepticism, once introductions were done. "...Yeah?" Bearly said, unsure what the correct answer was supposed to be. David said nothing further, took a long swig of his drink, and went back to whatever he'd been doing. Bearly left them to their conversation and went hunting for berries, where he met a new sort of slime entirely — small, and wearing, improbably, a tiny crown. He was so busy finding this adorable that he failed to block in time, took a nasty burn to the arm, very nearly dropped his sword out of fright, and — after several hours of far more caution than the slime's size seemed to warrant — finally finished it off. It left behind more of those strange coins. He carried them home, hoping Micah might have something for the burn, and instead found David Bobby leaning a half-built door against the clearing wall. "Just about to hang this," David said, beaming. "...What's going on here?" Bearly asked. "Couldn't let you keep sleeping in that old den, could I?" David shrugged, as though this answered everything, and went back to work. Bearly found Micah and asked, somewhat helplessly, why any of this was happening. Micah, without looking up from his book, only smiled. "Same reason he's about to help me build a proper shop. He just felt like it."

Bearly woke to laughter drifting through his new house — his house, he still hadn't quite gotten used to that word — and decided the first order of business was thanking David Bobby properly. Instead, he found Jasmine sitting cross-legged on a rug, eyes closed, apparently waiting for him. "Good morning," she said, without opening her eyes. "Just the bear I was hoping for. Do you happen to have more of those coins you gave to Micah?" Bearly produced a handful. Jasmine's eyes snapped open, and she was on her feet with startling grace. "Do you have any idea what you're holding?" she said. "This is what we call, at the university, an Ancient Coin. The last known one crumbled to dust years ago, back when the slime kings first began marching. We thought them lost to history. And you're carrying — several?" "This old thing?" Bearly said, looking down at it with the vague confusion of someone who has just been told his shoe is, in fact, a priceless artifact. Jasmine sighed the sigh of someone who has explained this concept to precisely the wrong audience. "This old thing is invaluable. Bring me more, and I'll teach you what's taught nowhere else but the university halls." She showed him, then and there, how to make a small sticky bomb — good, she said, for slowing a slime down long enough to run. Bearly thanked her, pocketed a few, and went back out — where the slimes, it turned out, were getting stranger by the day. One shot bolts of raw magic. Another simply vanished and reappeared somewhere else entirely. One hid behind another and, the instant its shield fell, took off at a dead sprint, glowing gold. Bearly, sensing an opportunity too shiny to pass up, chased it down — and came home with ten more coins, and, courtesy of Jasmine, a new trick: a vine-wrapped arrow of pure magic, fired from nowhere but his own two paws. "That," he said, admiring it, "is going to come in handy."

Some days are simply for eating lunch by a brook — fish, berries, a dollop of honey from a hive he'd only recently found — and wondering, idly, what the day might bring. What it brought was the strangest slime Bearly had yet encountered, one that seemed to change tactics every few seconds, as though it couldn't decide what kind of monster it wanted to be. He beat it eventually, more through stubbornness than skill, and returned to the clearing that evening with the distinct, uneasy sense that there were more people milling about than he remembered inviting. He was too tired to wonder about it properly, and so, sensibly, he simply went to bed instead — which is, on the whole, very good advice for anyone too tired to wonder about something properly. The next morning, he decided — with the sudden, stubborn determination of someone who has been putting something off for far too long — that today would be the day he finally found his way out of this forest. It was, in hindsight, a poor day to choose. He didn't retrace any of his usual cleared paths. He followed, instead, an old and overgrown trail he didn't recognize, tripped, slid down a small hill — and landed in the middle of more slimes than he had ever seen gathered in one place, several wearing crowns of their own. He fought his way back up that hill one slow, exhausting step at a time, and collapsed into bed the moment he made it home. "Well," he muttered, already half-asleep. "That definitely wasn't the right direction."

Somewhere else in the forest — closer than Bearly knew — a very different sort of meeting was underway. For the slimes, too, had a home, and it was under threat, and even slimes, it turns out, know how to be afraid of losing what's theirs. A rumble moved through the forest, and every creature in it, for one long moment, stopped to listen. The trees had been slowly turning green again these last few weeks — new leaves, new birdsong, the slow unmistakable feeling of a place remembering how to be alive. Almost everyone in the growing little village had noticed. Bearly, mostly, had not; he was still searching, quietly and every single day, for some path back to Frederick, back to the river, back to something he could recognize as before. He did not know that the Royal Slimes had gathered — all of them, every crowned and colored variety, united at last by a threat that had pushed clear to the edge of their own homeland: a monster who fought with magic and carried a blade sharper than fate itself. They had nearly trapped him once. He had slipped away. Today, they meant to end it. A scout returned, hopping excitedly, to say the monster was close. Bearly, following what he took for a golden butterfly, followed the scout instead — straight into a clearing ringed with slimes of every size the forest had to offer, crowned and uncrowned alike. He fought through the whole of that night and clear into the dawn, and when the very last slime finally fell, he dropped to his knees, out of breath, out of strength, and very nearly out of hope. The rustle that followed made him flinch. He turned, expecting the worst, too exhausted to properly defend himself — — and found Frederick instead, rushing across the clearing to wrap him, sweat and slime and all, in the tightest hug either of them could remember. "You're actually alive," Frederick breathed. It had taken him this long to find him. Stories had been drifting back to the village for weeks — a strange bear with a sword, living wild in the old forest; a merchant; a fisherman with remarkably good fish. Frederick had known, somehow, that his friend was tangled up in all of it, though he hadn't imagined this. He'd finally come looking, gotten lost twice, slept a night in a tree, and found Bearly at last on the morning the fighting finally stopped. The village doctor looked Bearly over and pronounced, with some confidence, that he would live. Bearly slept the better part of two days. When he finally woke, he sat by his window and looked out at a scene he only slowly recognized. Children were playing around the old stump. "I wonder," he murmured, "if I ought to tell them stories, the way people used to tell me." Then he blinked, and looked again. "...When did this become a village?"

And here, at last, we arrive at the part of the story that every good story is secretly about all along — not the sword, nor the slimes, nor even the butterfly, gold as it was, but the plain and quiet fact that Bearly never once set out to build anything at all. He'd only meant to find some berries. Everything else — Micah, and Henry, and David Bobby's door, and Jasmine's coins, and the whole small, stubborn, growing collection of people who had simply shown up and stayed — had happened somewhere in the gaps while Bearly was busy looking for something else entirely. Over a hot drink with Micah, it finally struck him properly: Frederick had found him. Which meant — "Micah," he said slowly, "your shop looks wonderful." Micah chuckled and clapped him on the shoulder. "David Bobby's doing, mostly. Rather a lot of hands helped, once people started arriving. Your friend's over at the Inn, by the way." "There's an Inn?" Bearly stepped outside, eyes going wide as saucers, and looked — properly looked, for the first time — at what had grown up around him. A sign now hung above the old stump: WELCOME TO WHISPERING GROVE. He read it. He smiled. He laughed, quietly, to himself. "Someone would have to be a little bit mad, to build a place here." Laughter answered him from just behind — Frederick, nearly doubled over, wheezing with it. Bearly laughed with him, until Frederick finally caught his breath enough to put both paws on his friend's shoulders. "Yes," Frederick said. "Yes, you are. And I'm glad you did it anyway." Bearly looked around at all of it — the slimes, the trees, the whole strange, unplanned shape of the place — and understood, all at once, that it had been here the entire time, waiting for him to notice. He hadn't meant to build a home. He'd only meant to find one. And somewhere in the looking, without ever quite deciding to, he had built one instead — not alone, but with every single person who had wandered in and simply stayed. Bearly rested a paw on the old sword at his side. It wasn't nearly as rusty as it used to be. "Hey, Frederick?" he asked, a little shyly. "Yes, Bearly?" "One of these days — will you tell me how to leave this forest? Not because I actually want to go. Just so I can bring people back here with me." Frederick chuckled, quiet and knowing. "Of course you've been lost this whole time. Took you long enough to catch it, though." Bearly smiled and turned toward the trees. "Yeah," he said. "Not what I was looking for. But I caught what I needed." And above them both, catching the last of the evening light, a single gold butterfly drifted in over the treetops — and, as butterflies do, disappeared.
